hero.title: Reading Your Mood Chart
hero.lead:
A mood chart is just your daily ratings plotted against time — but the first look at one is almost always misleading. The eye goes straight to the lowest point, and a chart read that way says "there's the bad day" and nothing else. Read properly, the same picture answers much better questions: where does my mood usually sit, how far does it swing, does it move on a schedule, and what actually travels with it?

This guide walks through those four readings in order — baseline, range, cycles, factors — with a worked example you can compare against your own. If you haven't started logging yet, begin with how to track your mood and come back in a couple of weeks.

sections.heading: Before you read: how much data do you need?
sections.html:
A chart of five days is a mood, not a pattern. Rough guidance on what different amounts of data can support:

  • 1–2 weeks: enough to see your rough baseline and whether your days vary a little or a lot. Not enough for any conclusion about a cause.
  • 3–6 weeks: weekly rhythms become visible, and strong single factors — sleep is usually the first — start to separate from noise.
  • 2–3 months: monthly and hormonal cycles, and slower drifts that a shorter window reads as random.
  • 6–12 months: seasonal shape, and the honest answer to "am I better than I was last year?"

Gaps are fine, as long as they are gaps rather than guesses. A week you didn't log is a blank; a week you reconstructed from memory quietly rewrites the chart in the direction of the story you already believe.

sections.heading: 1. Find your baseline
sections.html:
Your baseline is where your mood sits on an ordinary day — not the average of your best and worst days, but the level you keep returning to. On a chart, it's the band the line spends most of its time inside. On a 5-point scale, most people's baseline lands somewhere between 3 and 4.

Two things make the baseline the most useful number on the chart. First, it's the reference every other reading needs: a 3 means something completely different for someone who lives at 4 than for someone who lives at 2. Second, it moves slowly, so a shift in it is meaningful in a way that a single bad Tuesday is not. A baseline that has drifted from 4 to 3 over two months is a much bigger finding than any individual low point in that period — and it is exactly the kind of change that is invisible from the inside, because each day only feels slightly like the one before.

Practical way to read it: cover the extremes with your thumb and look at where the bulk of the line sits. Then compare this month's band to last month's. Direction matters more than the exact number.

sections.heading: 2. Judge the range
sections.html:
Range is how far your mood travels around that baseline — the vertical spread of the chart. Two people can share a baseline of 3.5 and have completely different experiences: one moves between 3 and 4 all month, the other bounces between 1 and 5 every few days. The average hides the thing that matters most.

Ask three questions of the spread:

  • How wide is a typical week? One point of movement is ordinary. Three or four points, repeatedly, is worth paying attention to.
  • How fast are the transitions? A slow slope down over a fortnight and a drop from 5 to 1 within a day are different phenomena, even if the low point is identical.
  • How long does a low last? A dip that recovers in a day or two behaves differently from one that sits at the bottom for two weeks.

If the swings are the main story in your chart, the guide on mood swings and their common contributors goes into what tends to drive them and when a pattern is worth raising with a professional.

sections.heading: 3. Look for cycles
sections.html:
Cycles are the most satisfying thing to find in a mood chart, because they turn "randomly bad sometimes" into something predictable — and something you can plan around. Four to check, in rough order of how quickly they show up:

  • Daily. Only visible if you log more than once a day. Consistently heavier mornings, or a reliable late-evening dip, is useful to know before you schedule hard conversations.
  • Weekly. The most common finding of all. Sunday evenings, Monday mornings, a Wednesday trough, a genuine Friday lift. Line your entries up by weekday and it usually jumps out within a month.
  • Monthly. Hormonal cycles produce some of the clearest patterns in mood data, and they need two or three months of dated entries before the shape is trustworthy.
  • Seasonal. Slow, and easy to attribute to whatever happened to be going on instead — which is exactly why the chart is better at spotting it than memory. See seasonal mood changes.

A caution: with enough data, cycles appear whether or not they're real. Before you trust one, check that it repeats at least three times and that you can name a plausible mechanism. "Low every third Thursday" with no explanation is usually coincidence.

sections.heading: 4. Factors: a worked example
sections.html:
This is where a mood chart stops describing and starts explaining — and where it's easiest to fool yourself. Here are two weeks of entries with mood, hours of sleep, and a short note:

DayMood (1–5)SleepNote
Mon36hBusy start
Tue25hLate night before
Wed25h30Flat, no reason
Thu48hSlept in
Fri47h30Walk, saw friends
Sat59h—
Sun38hDreading the week
Mon26hDeadline
Tue25hDeadline, no walk
Wed37hDeadline done
Thu48hGym
Fri47h—
Sat48h30Quiet day
Sun38hSunday feeling again

What this chart supports: a baseline around 3, a range of 2 to 5, a repeated Sunday dip, and a strong association between nights under six hours and mood at 2. That last one is worth acting on — it's consistent, it repeats, and there's an obvious mechanism.

What it does not prove: that short sleep caused the low mood. Both weeks had deadlines, and deadlines shorten sleep and flatten mood independently. Low mood also makes it harder to sleep, so the arrow may run backwards. And the Sunday dip has nothing to do with sleep at all — Sunday sleep was fine both weeks.

Turning a correlation into something you can trust

  1. Count the exceptions. Look for nights of good sleep followed by low mood, and vice versa. A factor with no exceptions in six weeks is a strong lead; one that holds half the time is a coincidence with good PR.
  2. Check the lag. Sleep usually shows up the next day, alcohol the next day, exercise the same day. If you're comparing same-day columns for a next-day effect, you'll miss it entirely.
  3. Look for the third thing. When two factors always move together, something upstream is often driving both. Deadlines, illness and travel are the usual culprits.
  4. Test it gently. One deliberate change at a time, held for two weeks, with everything else as normal. A personal experiment with a written record beats an opinion.

sections.heading: Paper chart vs app: an honest comparison
sections.html:
You can chart mood on graph paper, and a hand-drawn line has a certain honesty to it — plotting each point makes you look at the data instead of scrolling past it. A spreadsheet does more: sort by weekday, average by sleep bucket, and you can do most of what's described above.

What both cost you is the follow-through. Nobody re-sorts a spreadsheet by factor every month, and a paper chart can only show one comparison at a time — the one you drew. The app side of the trade:

  • Charts drawn as you log, over any period you choose, so the trend is always current instead of a project you keep meaning to do.
  • Mood broken down by factor — the sleep, activity and life-event comparisons above, without arithmetic, which makes it realistic to check a hunch in ten seconds rather than an evening.
  • Every point still attached to its note or photo, so a dip is one tap from the reason for it. A number without context is where charts go to be misread.
  • Apple Health sync, if you'd rather your sleep data arrive on its own than be typed in.
  • Export to PDF, XLSX, CSV or JSON — a PDF to bring to an appointment, or raw data if you want to do your own analysis.
  • AI insights over your own history, free with an optional premium tier, which read back what your entries suggest. Treat them as a second pair of eyes on the data, not as advice.

Whatever draws the chart, the interpretation stays yours — and a mood journal is a self-tracking tool rather than a diagnostic one. If the chart shows something that worries you, it's a very good thing to bring to a doctor or therapist, and a much more concrete starting point than trying to describe the last three months from memory.

items.question: How many weeks of data do I need before the chart is useful?
items.answer: **Three to four weeks** for weekly rhythms and strong single factors like sleep; **two to three months** for monthly cycles; **most of a year** for seasonal shape. One or two weeks will show you your baseline and roughly how much you vary, and that's already worth having.

items.question: My chart looks completely random. Am I doing it wrong?
items.answer: Probably not. Some charts are genuinely noisy, and a flat-looking scatter still tells you something real: your mood isn't being driven by one dominant factor. Try sorting entries by weekday, and check next-day effects rather than same-day ones — lagged patterns hide in plain sight. If it's still random after two months, that's an answer too.

items.question: Does a low point on my chart mean something is wrong?
items.answer: No. Everyone's chart has low points, and a bad day is not a diagnosis. What's worth attention is duration and direction: a low that persists most of the day for more than two weeks, or a baseline that's been drifting downward for months. Those are worth discussing with a doctor or therapist — bring the chart.

items.question: Should I average my mood ratings?
items.answer: A monthly average is a reasonable summary of the baseline, but don't stop there — averaging deliberately throws away the range, which is often the more interesting half of the story. Look at the average and the spread together, as described in the [mood swings guide](/mood-journal/mood-swings/).

items.question: Can I show my mood chart to a therapist?
items.answer: Yes, and most will welcome it. A dated chart with factor tags turns a vague summary into something specific to work from. Export to PDF for a clean version, or CSV/XLSX if they'd like the underlying numbers.

data.disclaimerText: This article is for general information only and is not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. A mood chart is a self-tracking tool, not a diagnostic instrument — patterns in it are a good starting point for a conversation with a doctor or therapist, never a substitute for one. If low mood persists most of the day for more than two weeks, or you notice lasting changes in sleep, appetite, or your ability to manage day to day, please speak to a healthcare professional. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, contact your local emergency services or a crisis helpline in your country right away — support is available now.
